tagline.text: Gold artifacts and dioramas that tell Philippine history, in the heart of Makati

children.text: Ayala Museum is a private museum in Makati that opened in 1967 and tells Philippine history in one place through more than 1,000 pre-colonial gold objects and 60 dioramas. It sits right next to Greenbelt, so it pairs easily with shopping and a meal for a half-day outing.

Ayala Museum sits in the middle of the Makati Central Business District, at the corner of Makati Avenue and De La Rosa Street beside Greenbelt Park. It opened in April 1967 as a project of the Filipinas Foundation (now the Ayala Foundation), first housed in the Insular Life Building, then moved in 1974 to the old Makati Stock Exchange Building. After that building was demolished in 2001, the current six-story building was built on the same site and dedicated on September 28, 2004. It was designed by the firm of the Filipino architect Leandro Locsin and is known for its solid look in granite, steel, and glass.

What makes this museum special for travelers is that it presents Philippine history in two very different ways. One is the Gold of Ancestors exhibition, which gathers gold ornaments and ceremonial objects made by people in the Philippines before the Spanish arrived. The other is the Diorama Experience, which uses 60 handmade dioramas to show events from prehistory to the modern era as scenes. Wikipedia lists more than 1,000 gold objects and 60 dioramas. Add A Millennium of Contact, with more than 500 Chinese and Southeast Asian ceramics, and even visitors who know little about history can grasp the big picture in a single day.

The building has six floors. The ground floor hosts changing exhibitions centered on contemporary art, the third floor has a gallery that rotates modern and contemporary Philippine art, and the sixth floor holds the Filipinas Heritage Library. The second-floor gallery is described as free to enter directly from the Greenbelt side, but floor operations can change, so check when you go. The museum closed for renovation from 2019 and reopened on December 4, 2021, so older visitor reviews may describe a different layout. First-time visitors should plan at least two hours and check the currently open exhibitions on the visitor map after entering.

The museum's roots are said to lie in the vision of the painter and collector Fernando Zóbel. In 2024 the Ayala Foundation marked the museum's 50th anniversary with the theme We Have History. From the 1970s to the 1990s the museum also put effort into conservation science and biological research, keeping an aviary and publishing the Filipinas Journal of Science and Culture. Today it is run by the Ayala Foundation's arts and culture division, and besides exhibitions it holds courses and workshops on history, contemporary art, music, creative writing, and design. Makati is the Philippines' largest commercial center and Greenbelt is a shopping and dining district, so it is easy to have lunch or coffee right after the museum. Because the exhibits are indoors, your plans hold up in heat or rain. Rather than trying to see everything at once, we recommend taking your time with the gold and the dioramas and looking at the rest if time allows.

More than 1,000 pieces are on display, including gold ornaments, ceremonial masks, chains, and vessels made across the Philippines before the Spanish colonial era. Lights can reflect off the gold and make photos glare, so read the label on what each object was used for first and then take your time. According to Wikipedia this is the museum's signature permanent exhibition, and it is the closest chance to see how prehistoric people worked gold and what they used it for.

Sixty handmade dioramas show key scenes from prehistory to modern history in order. Wikipedia describes them as covering history up to 1986. Many reviews say photography is allowed, but follow the instructions on site; it is the easiest introduction for anyone new to Philippine history.

More than 500 ceramics from China and Southeast Asia show that the Philippines has long been a stop on sea trade routes. Looking at the plates and jars by era shows what goods traveled back and forth.

The ground and third floors rotate exhibitions of contemporary art and modern paintings by Filipino artists. Because the shows differ with each visit, it helps to check the exhibition listings on the official site before you go.

The sixth-floor library is described as holding more than 13,000 contemporary volumes on Philippine arts, culture, and history, more than 2,000 rare titles, and more than 35,000 photographs. Its days are listed as Tuesday to Saturday, different from the museum, so check before you visit.
The Museum Cafe inside the museum is a place to rest before or after your visit. Many visitors also photograph the building's exterior and the installed sculptures from the Makati Avenue entrance.
The museum is known to offer a free digital guide through the Bloomberg Connects app. If you download the app in advance, you can follow English commentary as you tour.
Arrive at the museum, buy a ticket, and go in. Starting with the exhibits on the top floor and working down is a quieter route.
Take your time in the Gold of Ancestors exhibition. Read the labels to learn how the ornaments and ceremonial objects were used.
Move to the diorama exhibition and follow the scenes from prehistory to modern history.
Look around the A Millennium of Contact ceramics exhibition and the changing exhibitions currently on.
Head out to Greenbelt for lunch, and if time allows, walk through the mall and park.

The order of your visit may vary depending on which exhibitions are open. Pick up a visitor map when you enter, check the exhibitions on each floor, and prioritize your time on the gold and the dioramas. Hours and exhibitions can change, so check the visitor information on the official site before you leave.
Have breakfast at Greenbelt and wait for the museum to open.
Spend 2–3 hours at Ayala Museum.
Have lunch at a restaurant in central Makati.
Take a taxi or Grab to Bonifacio Global City and stroll its streets and malls.
Have dinner and return to your hotel.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), take a taxi or Grab to Makati. Depending on traffic it takes about
30 minutes–1.5 hours
Say Ayala Museum or Greenbelt Makati as your destination and drivers will understand.
From Intramuros or Malate, take a taxi or Grab to Makati. Roads back up at rush hour, so leave with time to spare.
You can also take the MRT-3 to Ayala Station and walk through central Makati. The streets are complicated, so check the walking distance and time on a map app.
Exact routes and fares can change, so check locally.
You can walk from the Greenbelt malls, and the museum entrance is on the Makati Avenue side.
For parking, use the Greenbelt basement lot or a lot inside the Ayala Center complex.
Ayala Museum is an indoor attraction, so you can visit any time of year. However, the roads into Makati get congested and wet in the rainy season, so travel is easier in the November–May dry season.
We recommend a weekday morning. Weekend and holiday afternoons can get crowded with families. The museum is closed on Mondays and holidays, so check before you go.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
Greenbelt, right next to the museum, has malls, restaurants, and cafes, so meals are no worry. It offers Korean, Japanese, and Filipino restaurants, so pick what suits your taste.

Hotels in central Makati are the closest to the museum. With a wide range of prices and easy access to shopping and nightlife, many travelers use it as a base for Manila. Room rates vary greatly by season, so check booking sites.

Walking along Makati Avenue from the museum leads to other malls and parks in the Ayala Center complex. Lunchtime is crowded, so plan for reservations or waiting. Restaurant names and prices change often, so checking when you arrive is the most accurate.
Admission fees change from time to time, so check the visitor information on the official site (ayalamuseum.org) first.
The museum is listed as closed on Mondays and holidays. It is said to open at 9 or 10 AM and close at 6 PM, Tuesday to Sunday, but sources differ, so check.
Gold objects can cause glare in photos because of the lighting. Try shooting from different angles.
Download the free digital guide on the Bloomberg Connects app in advance to make the exhibits easier to follow.
A full visit is said to take about 2 hours. It may run longer depending on your interests.
Free admission days require pre-registration and have limited time slots, so sign up early.
Greenbelt and Ayala Center are linked malls, so it is easy to walk between them even on rainy days.
Children under 12 also get the discounted rate, and the diorama exhibition is a good way for kids to understand history.
Fees, hours, and exhibitions differ by source and can change, so check the latest notices on the official site before your visit.
The museum is listed as closed on Mondays and holidays, so check if you plan a weekday visit.
The foreigner admission rate may be higher than the regular rate, so confirm the exact amount on site.
Follow on-site instructions for baggage storage and bag rules.
Roads into Makati are very congested at rush hour.
Exhibitions change often, so do not rely on old reviews.

Reach it by taxi to enjoy a modern cityscape and shopping.
A worthwhile museum to visit next if you want a deeper look at history and art.
